claim: Oxygenic photosynthesis supports virtually all life forms on earth.
source: Oxygenic photosynthesis supports virtually all life forms on earth.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about the fundamental role of oxygenic photosynthesis in supporting life.

claim: Light energy is converted by two photosystems—photosystem I (PSI) and photosystem II (PSII).
source: Light energy is converted by two photosystems—photosystem I (PSI) and photosystem II (PSII).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the photosynthetic apparatus.

claim: Nearly 50% of photosynthesis takes place in the Ocean.
source: Globally, nearly 50% of photosynthesis takes place in the Ocean, where single cell cyanobacteria and algae reside together with their viruses.
evidence: This is a quantitative statement about the global distribution of photosynthesis, representing established knowledge.

claim: An operon encoding PSI was identified in cyanobacterial marine viruses.
source: An operon encoding PSI was identified in cyanobacterial marine viruses.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work (Sharon et al., 2009) mentioned later in the manuscript.

claim: PSIPsaJF is promiscuous for its electron donors and can accept electrons from respiratory cytochromes.
source: PSIPsaJF is promiscuous for its electron donors and can accept electrons from respiratory cytochromes.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The structure of PSIPsaJF was solved.
source: We solved the structure of PSIPsaJF and a monomeric PSI, with subunit composition similar to the viral PSI, providing for the first time a detailed description of the reaction center and antenna system from mesophilic cyanobacteria, including red chlorophylls and cofactors of the electron transport chain.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by crystallographic data presented in Table 1 and structural figures.

claim: The structure of a monomeric PSI from Synechocystis was solved.
source: We solved the structure of PSIPsaJF and a monomeric PSI, with subunit composition similar to the viral PSI, providing for the first time a detailed description of the reaction center and antenna system from mesophilic cyanobacteria, including red chlorophylls and cofactors of the electron transport chain.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by crystallographic data presented in Table 1 and structural figures.

claim: This is the first detailed description of the reaction center and antenna system from mesophilic cyanobacteria.
source: We solved the structure of PSIPsaJF and a monomeric PSI, with subunit composition similar to the viral PSI, providing for the first time a detailed description of the reaction center and antenna system from mesophilic cyanobacteria, including red chlorophylls and cofactors of the electron transport chain.
evidence: This claim is supported by the novelty of the structural data presented and comparison to existing structures from thermophilic organisms.

claim: Oxygenic photosynthesis takes place in cyanobacteria, algae, and plants.
source: Oxygenic photosynthesis, which takes place in cyanobacteria, algae, and plants, provides most of the food and fuel on Earth (Barber, 2004; Nelson, 2011).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Oxygenic photosynthesis provides most of the food and fuel on Earth.
source: Oxygenic photosynthesis, which takes place in cyanobacteria, algae, and plants, provides most of the food and fuel on Earth (Barber, 2004; Nelson, 2011).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: PSII mediates the extraction of electrons from water to the plastoquinone pool.
source: Cyanobacterial photosynthetic membranes contain two photosystems, of which PSII mediates the extraction of electrons from water, the initial electron donor, to the plastoquinone pool.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the function of PSII.

claim: PSI mediates electron transfer from cytochrome C553 (or plastocyanin in eukaryotes) to ferredoxin.
source: PSI mediates electron transfer from cytochrome C553 (or plastocyanin in eukaryotes) to ferredoxin, thereby generating the reducing power needed for CO2 fixation in the form of NADPH.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the function of PSI.

claim: PSI generates the reducing power needed for CO2 fixation in the form of NADPH.
source: PSI mediates electron transfer from cytochrome C553 (or plastocyanin in eukaryotes) to ferredoxin, thereby generating the reducing power needed for CO2 fixation in the form of NADPH.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the function of PSI.

claim: The architecture of oxygenic photosynthesis in cyanobacteria has largely been determined.
source: The architecture of oxygenic photosynthesis in cyanobacteria has largely been determined and the structures of both photosystems from thermophilic cyanobacteria have been solved at high resolution (Jordan et al., 2001; Ferreira et al., 2004; Nelson and Ben-Shem, 2004; Amunts et al., 2007; Umena et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field, supported by multiple citations.

claim: The structures of both photosystems from thermophilic cyanobacteria have been solved at high resolution.
source: The architecture of oxygenic photosynthesis in cyanobacteria has largely been determined and the structures of both photosystems from thermophilic cyanobacteria have been solved at high resolution (Jordan et al., 2001; Ferreira et al., 2004; Nelson and Ben-Shem, 2004; Amunts et al., 2007; Umena et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a statement about prior structural work, supported by multiple citations.

claim: Photosynthetic reaction centers are classified according to their terminal electron acceptor as either type I or type II.
source: Photosynthetic reaction centers are classified according to their terminal electron acceptor as either type I, with an iron sulfur cluster acceptor, or type II, with a quinone terminal acceptor.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the classification of reaction centers.

claim: Type I reaction centers have an iron sulfur cluster acceptor.
source: Photosynthetic reaction centers are classified according to their terminal electron acceptor as either type I, with an iron sulfur cluster acceptor, or type II, with a quinone terminal acceptor.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about type I reaction centers.

claim: Type II reaction centers have a quinone terminal acceptor.
source: Photosynthetic reaction centers are classified according to their terminal electron acceptor as either type I, with an iron sulfur cluster acceptor, or type II, with a quinone terminal acceptor.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about type II reaction centers.

claim: PSI presumably evolved from simpler homodimeric bacterial reaction centers.
source: PSI, a type I reaction center, presumably evolved from the simpler homodimeric bacterial reaction centers (Buttner et al., 1992; Liebl et al., 1993; Baymann et al., 2001; Nelson and Ben-Shem, 2005).
evidence: This is an inference about evolutionary history supported by citations.

claim: There are currently only two known versions of type I reaction centers.
source: We currently know only two versions of the type I reaction centers: the relatively simple bacterial homodimer found in green sulfur bacteria (GSB), heliobacteria and Chloracidobacterium or the much more complex PSI with its 11–15 subunits found in cyanobacteria and all photosynthetic eukaryotes (Buttner et al., 1992; Hauska et al., 2001; Nelson and Yocum, 2006).
evidence: This is a statement about the known diversity of type I reaction centers, supported by citations.

claim: The bacterial homodimer type I reaction center is found in green sulfur bacteria, heliobacteria and Chloracidobacterium.
source: We currently know only two versions of the type I reaction centers: the relatively simple bacterial homodimer found in green sulfur bacteria (GSB), heliobacteria and Chloracidobacterium or the much more complex PSI with its 11–15 subunits found in cyanobacteria and all photosynthetic eukaryotes (Buttner et al., 1992; Hauska et al., 2001; Nelson and Yocum, 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the distribution of type I reaction centers, supported by citations.

claim: PSI with its 11–15 subunits is found in cyanobacteria and all photosynthetic eukaryotes.
source: We currently know only two versions of the type I reaction centers: the relatively simple bacterial homodimer found in green sulfur bacteria (GSB), heliobacteria and Chloracidobacterium or the much more complex PSI with its 11–15 subunits found in cyanobacteria and all photosynthetic eukaryotes (Buttner et al., 1992; Hauska et al., 2001; Nelson and Yocum, 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the distribution of PSI, supported by citations.

claim: Sequence conservation between the PsaA/B subunits of PSI and the single large subunit of the homodimeric reaction centers is low.
source: Although sequence conservation between the PsaA/B subunits of PSI and the single large subunit of the homodimeric reaction centers is low, their inferred membrane topology is similar, and the sequence conservation around the bound iron sulfur cluster is high, supporting the notion of a common ancestor (Mulkidjanian and Junge, 1997; Blankenship and Hartman, 1998; Baymann et al., 2001; Mazor et al., 2012; Rutherford et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a statement about sequence analysis supported by citations.

claim: The inferred membrane topology of PsaA/B subunits and the single large subunit of homodimeric reaction centers is similar.
source: Although sequence conservation between the PsaA/B subunits of PSI and the single large subunit of the homodimeric reaction centers is low, their inferred membrane topology is similar, and the sequence conservation around the bound iron sulfur cluster is high, supporting the notion of a common ancestor (Mulkidjanian and Junge, 1997; Blankenship and Hartman, 1998; Baymann et al., 2001; Mazor et al., 2012; Rutherford et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a statement about structural similarity supported by citations.

claim: Sequence conservation around the bound iron sulfur cluster is high between PSI and homodimeric reaction centers.
source: Although sequence conservation between the PsaA/B subunits of PSI and the single large subunit of the homodimeric reaction centers is low, their inferred membrane topology is similar, and the sequence conservation around the bound iron sulfur cluster is high, supporting the notion of a common ancestor (Mulkidjanian and Junge, 1997; Blankenship and Hartman, 1998; Baymann et al., 2001; Mazor et al., 2012; Rutherford et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a statement about sequence conservation supported by citations.

claim: PSI and homodimeric reaction centers share a common ancestor.
source: Although sequence conservation between the PsaA/B subunits of PSI and the single large subunit of the homodimeric reaction centers is low, their inferred membrane topology is similar, and the sequence conservation around the bound iron sulfur cluster is high, supporting the notion of a common ancestor (Mulkidjanian and Junge, 1997; Blankenship and Hartman, 1998; Baymann et al., 2001; Mazor et al., 2012; Rutherford et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an inference about evolutionary relationships supported by citations and structural/sequence data.

claim: In the earth's oceans, mainly single cell organisms, cyanobacteria or algae, perform oxygenic photosynthesis.
source: In the earth ocean's, mainly single cell organisms, cyanobacteria or algae, perform oxygenic photosynthesis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about marine photosynthesis.

claim: Marine viruses are involved in cyanobacterial photosynthesis.
source: One of the most intriguing aspects of marine cyanobacterial photosynthesis is the involvement of various viruses in the process.
evidence: This is supported by the presence of photosynthetic genes in viral genomes as cited in the manuscript.

claim: Photosynthetic genes are present in viral genomes.
source: Hints on this involvement come from the presence of photosynthetic genes in viral genomes (Mann et al., 2003; Sullivan et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Many marine phages encode for either the D1 gene or both D1 and D2.
source: Many marine phages encode for either the D1 gene or both D1 and D2 which together make up the reaction center of PSII (Sullivan et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: D1 and D2 together make up the reaction center of PSII.
source: Many marine phages encode for either the D1 gene or both D1 and D2 which together make up the reaction center of PSII (Sullivan et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge about PSII structure.

claim: Several subunits of the NDH1 complex are found in the viral metagenome.
source: In addition, several subunits of the NDH1 complex and soluble cytochromes are also found in the viral metagenome (Philosof et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Soluble cytochromes are found in the viral metagenome.
source: In addition, several subunits of the NDH1 complex and soluble cytochromes are also found in the viral metagenome (Philosof et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Marine viruses have the ability to alter the host photosynthesis pathways.
source: The presence of these genes suggests that marine viruses have the ability to alter the host photosynthesis pathways in ways, which are still not completely understood.
evidence: This is an inference based on the presence of photosynthetic genes in viral genomes.

claim: An operon encoding a complete, albeit minimal, PSI complex was found in the genome of several marine cyanophages.
source: Recently, an operon encoding a complete, albeit minimal, PSI complex was found in the genome of several marine cyanophages (Sharon et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The viral PSI has a unique gene composition compared to the PSI composition of its hosts.
source: The viral PSI has a unique gene composition compared to the PSI composition of its hosts.
evidence: This is supported by the description of missing genes and fusion proteins in the viral PSI.

claim: PsaL and PsaI are missing from the viral PSI.
source: PsaL and PsaI are missing and a unique PsaJ-PsaF (PsaJF) fusion-protein exists.
evidence: This is a description of the viral PSI gene composition based on genomic analysis.

claim: A unique PsaJ-PsaF (PsaJF) fusion-protein exists in the viral PSI.
source: PsaL and PsaI are missing and a unique PsaJ-PsaF (PsaJF) fusion-protein exists.
evidence: This is a description of the viral PSI gene composition based on genomic analysis.

claim: The absence of both PsaL and PsaI from the viral PSI suggests that it functions as a monomer.
source: The absence of both PsaL and PsaI from the viral PSI suggests that it functions as a monomer and does not assemble trimers since both PsaL and PsaI are important for the formation of the cyanobacterial trimer (Chitnis and Chitnis, 1993; Xu et al., 1995).
evidence: This is an inference based on the known roles of PsaL and PsaI in trimer formation, supported by citations.

claim: Both PsaL and PsaI are important for the formation of the cyanobacterial trimer.
source: The absence of both PsaL and PsaI from the viral PSI suggests that it functions as a monomer and does not assemble trimers since both PsaL and PsaI are important for the formation of the cyanobacterial trimer (Chitnis and Chitnis, 1993; Xu et al., 1995).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: In eukaryotes, the PsaF subunit is important for electron transfer between plastocyanin (PC) and the PSI complex.
source: In eukaryotes, the PsaF subunit is important for electron transfer between plastocyanin (PC) and the PSI complex (Farah et al., 1995; Hippler et al., 1996).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The structures of PsaF from cyanobacteria and plants are very similar.
source: Although the structures of PsaF from cyanobacteria and plants are very similar, the role of PsaF is less well defined in cyanobacteria (Chitnis et al., 1991; Xu et al., 1994a, 1994b; Hippler et al., 1996).
evidence: This is a statement about structural similarity supported by citations.

claim: The role of PsaF is less well defined in cyanobacteria.
source: Although the structures of PsaF from cyanobacteria and plants are very similar, the role of PsaF is less well defined in cyanobacteria (Chitnis et al., 1991; Xu et al., 1994a, 1994b; Hippler et al., 1996).
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The N-terminus of PsaF forms a major 'bump' in the flat, luminal side of PSI.
source: Structurally, the N-terminus of PsaF forms a major 'bump' in the flat, luminal side of PSI.
evidence: This is a structural description based on known PSI structures.

claim: The eukaryotic PsaF contains several additional positively charged residues that stabilize the interaction between PSI and PC.
source: Within this domain, the eukaryotic PsaF contains several additional positively charged residues that stabilize the interaction between PSI and PC (Farah et al., 1995; Hippler et al., 1996).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: In the viral PSI the N-terminus of PsaF is deleted.
source: In the viral PSI the N-terminus of PsaF is deleted and as a result the luminal face of PSI is expected to be relatively flat.
evidence: This is a description of the viral PSI structure based on genomic analysis.

claim: The luminal face of viral PSI is expected to be relatively flat.
source: In the viral PSI the N-terminus of PsaF is deleted and as a result the luminal face of PSI is expected to be relatively flat.
evidence: This is an inference based on the deletion of the N-terminus of PsaF.

claim: There is a very high degree of structural conservation in PSI complexes.
source: The unique light harvesting and transfer requirements, together with the large number of interconnected subunits, have resulted in a very high degree of structural conservation in PSI complexes (Ben-Shem et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a statement about structural conservation supported by citation.

claim: Approximately 90 chlorophyll molecules bound by the PSI reaction center remained largely unmoved by more than 2 billion years of evolution between Thermosynechococcus elongatus and Pisum sativum.
source: For example, approximately 90 chlorophyll molecules, bound by the PSI reaction center remained largely unmoved by more than 2 billion years of evolution between the thermophilic cyanobacterium Thermosynechococcus elongatus and the flowering plant Pisum sativum (Jordan et al., 2001; Ben-Shem et al., 2003; Amunts et al., 2007, 2010).
evidence: This is a statement about structural conservation supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: A common feature of PSI is the presence of low energy chlorophyll molecules called 'red chlorophylls'.
source: A common feature of PSI is the presence of low energy chlorophyll molecules called 'red chlorophylls'.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PSI.

claim: Red chlorophylls are present in the reaction center of cyanobacteria.
source: Red chlorophylls are present in the reaction center of cyanobacteria and in the light-harvesting belt of the plant PSI.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the distribution of red chlorophylls.

claim: Red chlorophylls are present in the light-harvesting belt of the plant PSI.
source: Red chlorophylls are present in the reaction center of cyanobacteria and in the light-harvesting belt of the plant PSI.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the distribution of red chlorophylls.

claim: In cyanobacteria, red chlorophylls can affect the trapping kinetics of excitation energy.
source: In cyanobacteria, red chlorophylls can affect the trapping kinetics of excitation energy as shown by measurements done on PSI from various species (Gobets et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to experimental work.

claim: The location of the red chlorophylls within the internal antenna of PSI is still a matter of debate.
source: The location of the red chlorophylls within the internal antenna of PSI is still a matter of debate, the inter species variability of the red absorption suggests that they are located in a relatively variable region of PSI.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The inter species variability of the red absorption suggests that red chlorophylls are located in a relatively variable region of PSI.
source: The location of the red chlorophylls within the internal antenna of PSI is still a matter of debate, the inter species variability of the red absorption suggests that they are located in a relatively variable region of PSI.
evidence: This is an inference based on observed variability in red absorption.

claim: All calculations of individual pigment energies are currently based on the high resolution PSI structure from Thermosynechococcus elongatus.
source: Currently, all the calculations of individual pigment energies are based on the high resolution PSI structure from Thermosynechococcus elongatus, which contains a relatively large number of red pigments.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of computational studies.

claim: Thermosynechococcus elongatus PSI contains a relatively large number of red pigments.
source: Currently, all the calculations of individual pigment energies are based on the high resolution PSI structure from Thermosynechococcus elongatus, which contains a relatively large number of red pigments.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Thermosynechococcus PSI.

claim: New, high resolution structures are needed to compare antenna system across various species.
source: New, high resolution structures are needed to compare antenna system across various species.
evidence: This is a statement about the need for additional structural data.

claim: The fused subunit PsaJF is incorporated into the PSI complex.
source: We find that the fused subunit PsaJF is incorporated into the PSI complex and that this incorporation results in a promiscuous PSI, able to accept electrons from respiratory cytochromes.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The incorporation of PsaJF results in a promiscuous PSI, able to accept electrons from respiratory cytochromes.
source: We find that the fused subunit PsaJF is incorporated into the PSI complex and that this incorporation results in a promiscuous PSI, able to accept electrons from respiratory cytochromes.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The trimer to monomer ratio is similar in both wild-type and PsaJF strains.
source: After purifying the PSI complex from the photosynthetic membranes of both wild-type and PsaJF strains, we found that the trimer to monomer ratio is similar in both strains, indicating that the assembly and stability of PSIPsaJF is not disturbed (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The assembly and stability of PSIPsaJF is not disturbed.
source: After purifying the PSI complex from the photosynthetic membranes of both wild-type and PsaJF strains, we found that the trimer to monomer ratio is similar in both strains, indicating that the assembly and stability of PSIPsaJF is not disturbed (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is an inference based on the similar trimer to monomer ratios observed.

claim: The purified PSIPsaJF complex contained the fused PsaJF subunit in lieu of PsaJ and PsaF.
source: The subunit composition of the purified complex showed that it indeed contained the fused PsaJF subunit in lieu of PsaJ and PsaF (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: PSIPsaJF was crystallized and diffraction data to 3.8 Å resolution was obtained.
source: To get a more detailed view of the PsaJF subunit in PSIPsaJF, we crystallized PSIPsaJF and obtained diffraction data to 3.8 Å resolution (Table 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by crystallographic data presented in Table 1.

claim: The crystal structure of the PSIPsaJF complex was solved by molecular replacement.
source: The crystal structure of the PSIPsaJF complex was solved by molecular replacement, first by using the previously determined cyanobacterial structure as a search model (PDB ID 1JBO) and later with a higher resolution model from Synechocystis (see 'Results' below).
evidence: This is a description of the method used to solve the structure.

claim: The model reveals three monomers in the asymmetric unit.
source: The model reveals three monomers in the asymmetric unit.
evidence: This is a structural finding from the crystallographic analysis.

claim: A complete trimeric complex is formed from monomers positioned in three unit cells.
source: A complete trimeric complex is formed from monomers positioned in three unit cells (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a structural finding from the crystallographic analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The overall architecture of PSI from Synechocystis is highly similar to the Thermosynechococcus elongatus PSI.
source: As seen in Figure 2A,B, the overall architecture of PSI from Synechocystis is highly similar to the Thermosynechococcus elongatus PSI with two noticeable exceptions, the fused PsaJF subunit and PsaX, which as expected, is missing (the genome of Synechocystis PCC6803 does not contain a PsaX homolog).
evidence: This is a structural comparison based on the crystal structures.

claim: PsaX is missing from Synechocystis PSI.
source: As seen in Figure 2A,B, the overall architecture of PSI from Synechocystis is highly similar to the Thermosynechococcus elongatus PSI with two noticeable exceptions, the fused PsaJF subunit and PsaX, which as expected, is missing (the genome of Synechocystis PCC6803 does not contain a PsaX homolog).
evidence: This is a structural finding supported by genomic information.

claim: The genome of Synechocystis PCC6803 does not contain a PsaX homolog.
source: As seen in Figure 2A,B, the overall architecture of PSI from Synechocystis is highly similar to the Thermosynechococcus elongatus PSI with two noticeable exceptions, the fused PsaJF subunit and PsaX, which as expected, is missing (the genome of Synechocystis PCC6803 does not contain a PsaX homolog).
evidence: This is genomic information about Synechocystis.

claim: Deleting the N-terminus of PsaF resulted in a flattened plateau on the luminal side of the complex.
source: Deleting the N-terminus of PsaF resulted in a flattened plateau on the luminal side of the complex (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This is a structural finding from the crystal structure shown in Figure 2B,C.

claim: Three chlorophyll molecules and four carotenoids are coordinated by PsaJ and PsaF in the Thermosynechococcus PSI structure.
source: Three chlorophyll molecules and four carotenoids are coordinated by PsaJ and PsaF in the Thermosynechococcus PSI structure (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a structural description from the Thermosynechococcus PSI structure.

claim: All of the ligands coordinated by PsaJ and PsaF in Thermosynechococcus are probably lost during the assembly of PSIPsaJF.
source: We find that all of these ligands are probably lost during the assembly of PSIPsaJF and could not be traced in our model (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a structural finding from the PSIPsaJF crystal structure.

claim: The overall organization of the other cofactors in PSI is hardly affected in PSIPsaJF.
source: In spite of the relatively low resolution, we find that the overall organization of the other cofactors in PSI is hardly affected in PSIPsaJF demonstrating the mild effect of the JF mutation on the overall organization and integrity of the complex.
evidence: This is a structural finding from the PSIPsaJF crystal structure.

claim: The JF mutation has a mild effect on the overall organization and integrity of the complex.
source: In spite of the relatively low resolution, we find that the overall organization of the other cofactors in PSI is hardly affected in PSIPsaJF demonstrating the mild effect of the JF mutation on the overall organization and integrity of the complex.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural findings.

claim: PSIPsaJF is reduced by its native electron donor cytochrome c553 with similar kinetics compared to the wild-type PSI.
source: However, PSIPsaJF is reduced by its native electron donor cytochrome c553 (CytC553) with similar kinetics compared to the wild-type PSI (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: In eukaryotic PSI, the N-terminus of PsaF was shown to be important for the electron donation reaction between plastocyanin and PSI.
source: This is in contrast to eukaryotic PSI where the N-terminus of PsaF was shown to be important for the electron donation reaction between plastocyanin and PSI (Hippler et al., 1996).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The similar electron donation rates observed with CytC553 are in agreement with previously published results obtained from PsaF and PsaJ deleted strains.
source: The similar electron donation rates observed with CytC553 are in agreement with previously published results obtained from PsaF and PsaJ deleted strains (Xu et al., 1994a, 1994b).
evidence: This is a comparison to prior work supported by citation.

claim: PSIPsaJF had faster cytochrome oxidation kinetics when respiratory cytochrome was used compared to the wild-type complex.
source: Compared to the wild-type complex, PSIPsaJF had faster cytochrome oxidation kinetics when respiratory cytochrome was used (Figure 3C), and similar kinetics when native CytC553 was used (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: PSIPsaJF had similar cytochrome oxidation kinetics when native CytC553 was used compared to the wild-type complex.
source: Compared to the wild-type complex, PSIPsaJF had faster cytochrome oxidation kinetics when respiratory cytochrome was used (Figure 3C), and similar kinetics when native CytC553 was used (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Wild-type and PSIPsaJF strains have similar cellular growth rates.
source: The similarity between the reaction kinetics of PSI reduction together with the similar cellular growth rates of wild-type and PSIPsaJF strains shows that deleting the N-terminus of PsaF causes no gross perturbation to the interaction between PSI and CytC553, that is, the N-terminus of PsaF does not play any positive role in this interaction in Synechocystis.
evidence: This is an experimental observation mentioned in the text.

claim: Deleting the N-terminus of PsaF causes no gross perturbation to the interaction between PSI and CytC553.
source: The similarity between the reaction kinetics of PSI reduction together with the similar cellular growth rates of wild-type and PSIPsaJF strains shows that deleting the N-terminus of PsaF causes no gross perturbation to the interaction between PSI and CytC553, that is, the N-terminus of PsaF does not play any positive role in this interaction in Synechocystis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data.

claim: The N-terminus of PsaF does not play any positive role in the interaction between PSI and CytC553 in Synechocystis.
source: The similarity between the reaction kinetics of PSI reduction together with the similar cellular growth rates of wild-type and PSIPsaJF strains shows that deleting the N-terminus of PsaF causes no gross perturbation to the interaction between PSI and CytC553, that is, the N-terminus of PsaF does not play any positive role in this interaction in Synechocystis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data.

claim: The N-terminus of PsaF can act as a negative regulator of some electron donation reactions, especially from positively charged donors such as respiratory cytochromes.
source: The N-terminus of PsaF can act as a negative regulator of some electron donation reactions, especially from positively charged donors such as respiratory cytochromes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing increased promiscuity in PSIPsaJF.

claim: The negative regulatory function was the original function of PsaF in a more primitive form of PSI.
source: We suggest that this was the original function of PsaF in a more primitive form of PSI and only later, as PSI evolved, the binding site was refined to its final configuration.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the evolutionary history of PsaF.

claim: In the viral PSI, promiscuity can be beneficial when the viral reaction center encounters the highly variable cytochromes found in marine cyanobacteria.
source: In the viral PSI, such promiscuity can be beneficial when the viral reaction center encounters the highly variable cytochromes found in marine cyanobacteria (Mazor et al., 2012) or alternatively to allow PSI to accept electrons from respiratory activities when PSII activity is compromised.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the functional advantage of viral PSI promiscuity.

claim: Marine cyanobacteria contain highly variable cytochromes.
source: In the viral PSI, such promiscuity can be beneficial when the viral reaction center encounters the highly variable cytochromes found in marine cyanobacteria (Mazor et al., 2012) or alternatively to allow PSI to accept electrons from respiratory activities when PSII activity is compromised.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Viral PSI promiscuity may allow PSI to accept electrons from respiratory activities when PSII activity is compromised.
source: In the viral PSI, such promiscuity can be beneficial when the viral reaction center encounters the highly variable cytochromes found in marine cyanobacteria (Mazor et al., 2012) or alternatively to allow PSI to accept electrons from respiratory activities when PSII activity is compromised.

evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The function of the native, bacterial NDH-I complex in cyclic electron flow is established.
source: This is the case with the virally encoded NDH-I subunits, where the function of the native, bacterial complex in cyclic electron flow is established.
evidence: This is established knowledge about NDH-I function.

claim: A phage specific mutation, removal of the N-terminus of PsaF, results in a promiscuous PSI complex.
source: In this study, we show that a phage specific mutation, removal of the N-terminus of PsaF, results in a promiscuous PSI complex.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data.

claim: The properties of the small electron donor (either PC or CytC553) largely determine its mode of interaction with PSI.
source: It is known that the properties of the small electron donor (either PC or CytC553) largely determine its mode of interaction with PSI (Hervas et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Marine cyanobacteria contain an especially diverse set of soluble cytochromes with variable physical properties.
source: Marine cyanobacteria contain an especially diverse set of soluble cytochromes with variable physical properties (Mazor et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Photosynthesis performed during phage infection is catalyzed (at least partially) by phage proteins.
source: However, our findings suggest that photosynthesis performed during phage infection and catalyzed (at least partially) by phage proteins ('Viral photosynthesis') utilize very different cytochromes efficiently and will not be sensitive to the nature of the electron donor.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings.

claim: Viral photosynthesis utilizes very different cytochromes efficiently and will not be sensitive to the nature of the electron donor.
source: However, our findings suggest that photosynthesis performed during phage infection and catalyzed (at least partially) by phage proteins ('Viral photosynthesis') utilize very different cytochromes efficiently and will not be sensitive to the nature of the electron donor.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings.

claim: The existence of both NDH-I subunits and a promiscuous PSI operon in a single phage genome suggests that cyclic electron flow is enhanced during phage replication.
source: The existence of both NDH-I subunits and a promiscuous PSI operon in a single phage genome suggests that cyclic electron flow is enhanced during phage replication (Philosof et al., 2011).
evidence: This is an inference based on the genomic composition of phages, supported by citation.

claim: Enhanced cyclic electron flow during phage replication can be achieved by increasing the flow of electrons into the photosynthetic electron transport chain through the NDH–I complex.
source: This can be achieved by increasing the flow of electrons into the photosynthetic electron transport chain through the NDH–I complex or by utilizing electrons from respiratory cytochromes or both.
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism of enhanced cyclic electron flow.

claim: Enhanced cyclic electron flow during phage replication can be achieved by utilizing electrons from respiratory cytochromes.
source: This can be achieved by increasing the flow of electrons into the photosynthetic electron transport chain through the NDH–I complex or by utilizing electrons from respiratory cytochromes or both.
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism of enhanced cyclic electron flow.

claim: The suggested function of virally encoded D1 and D2 is to replenish the rapidly damaged host D1 and D2 proteins during infection.
source: The suggested function of virally encoded D1 and D2 is to replenish the rapidly damaged host D1 and D2 proteins during infection (Mann et al., 2003; Alperovitch-Lavy et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from prior work supported by citations.

claim: Some basal level of linear electron flow in the cells probably plays a major part in phage multiplication.
source: This seems to partially contradict the notion of increased cyclic electron flow in infected cells but it is probable that some basal level of linear electron flow in the cells plays a major part in phage multiplication.
evidence: This is a speculation to reconcile different observations.

claim: The phage-encoded PSI complex with its unique gene composition adds an important step to the scenario of PSI evolution from a primordial homodimeric entity to the current highly evolved complexes.
source: We suggest that the phage-encoded PSI complex with its unique gene composition adds an important step to the scenario of PSI evolution from a primordial homodimeric entity to the current highly evolved complexes (Nelson, 2011; Mazor et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a speculation about evolutionary history supported by citations.

claim: The formation of the primordial heterodimer allowed for the evolution of the unique properties of the peripheral subunits.
source: In this scenario, the formation of the primordial heterodimer allowed for the evolution of the unique properties of the peripheral subunits, trimer formation in the case of PsaL and interaction with electron donors in the case of PsaF.
evidence: This is a speculation about evolutionary history.

claim: The specificity and complexity of biological machines increases along their evolutionary path.
source: The specificity and complexity of biological machines increases along their evolutionary path and PSI is a prime example of this property.
evidence: This is a general principle about evolution applied to PSI.

claim: Cyanobacterial PSI is much more complicated and intricate than its ancestral homodimer.
source: Cyanobacterial PSI is much more complicated and intricate than its ancestral homodimer and the plant PSI adds additional levels of complexity over the cyanobacterial complex.
evidence: This is a statement about the evolutionary complexity of PSI.

claim: Plant PSI adds additional levels of complexity over the cyanobacterial complex.
source: Cyanobacterial PSI is much more complicated and intricate than its ancestral homodimer and the plant PSI adds additional levels of complexity over the cyanobacterial complex.
evidence: This is a statement about the evolutionary complexity of PSI.

claim: The preservation of simpler forms of PSI is quite unique and stems from the relatively simple life cycle of phages.
source: The preservation of simpler forms of PSI is therefore quite unique and stems from the relatively simple life cycle of phages and from the unique evolutionary requirements associated with this life cycle.
evidence: This is an inference about the evolutionary preservation of viral PSI.

claim: Some marine phages from the Myoviridae family can infect different species of cyanobacteria.
source: For example, some marine phages from the Myoviridae family can infect different species of cyanobacteria (Sullivan et al., 2003) and this creates unique requirements on their genes such as utilizing the different chlorophyll species found in Prochlorococcus and Synechococcus.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The ability of some phages to infect different species creates unique requirements on their genes such as utilizing the different chlorophyll species found in Prochlorococcus and Synechococcus.
source: For example, some marine phages from the Myoviridae family can infect different species of cyanobacteria (Sullivan et al., 2003) and this creates unique requirements on their genes such as utilizing the different chlorophyll species found in Prochlorococcus and Synechococcus.
evidence: This is an inference about the evolutionary pressures on phage genes.

claim: The viral complex preserves some of the properties of the common PSI ancestor, lost from both the cyanobacterial and plant PSI.
source: The viral complex preserves some of the properties of the common PSI ancestor, lost from both the cyanobacterial and plant PSI.
evidence: This is an inference about the evolutionary significance of viral PSI.

claim: One of the ancestral properties preserved in viral PSI is promiscuity for electron donors as exemplified by the fused PsaJF subunit.
source: One of these properties appears to be promiscuity for electron donors as exemplified by the fused PsaJF subunit.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings.

claim: Further sampling of ocean genomic surveys will reveal further examples of ancestral forms of PSI and other unique versions of highly conserved genes.
source: The incredible richness uncovered by ocean genomic surveys suggests that further sampling will reveal further examples of ancestral forms of PSI and other unique versions of highly conserved genes.
evidence: This is a speculation about future discoveries.

claim: The two structures described provide the first detailed look at the Synechocystis PSI complex.
source: The two structures described in this work provide the first detailed look at the Synechocystis PSI complex.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the work.

claim: The two most prominent differences between Synechocystis and Thermosynechococcus are the longer trapping time for excitation energy and the stronger red absorbance found in Thermosynechococcus.
source: The two most prominent differences between Synechocystis and Thermosynechococcus are the longer trapping time for excitation energy and the stronger red absorbance found in Thermosynechococcus.
evidence: This is a statement about known differences between the two organisms.

claim: Both the longer trapping time and stronger red absorbance differences are probably related to the number of red-shifted pigments found in PSI.
source: Both of these differences are probably related to the number of red-shifted pigments found in PSI.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known properties of red chlorophylls.

claim: This study provides definite proof for the absence of the putative 'red' chlorophyll trimer in Synechocystis.
source: This study provides definite proof for the absence of the putative 'red' chlorophyll trimer in Synechocystis and narrowed the number of coupled pigment dimers to two.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the structural data.

claim: This study narrowed the number of coupled pigment dimers to two.
source: This study provides definite proof for the absence of the putative 'red' chlorophyll trimer in Synechocystis and narrowed the number of coupled pigment dimers to two.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the structural data.

claim: The Synechocystis PSI complex revealed the PsaX-less conformation of the antenna.
source: Structurally, the Synechocystis PSI complex revealed the PsaX-less conformation of the antenna and it is evident that this configuration is closer to the plant PSI inner antenna and thus can be considered the ancestral arrangement.
evidence: This is a structural finding from the crystal structure.

claim: The PsaX-less conformation is closer to the plant PSI inner antenna and thus can be considered the ancestral arrangement.
source: Structurally, the Synechocystis PSI complex revealed the PsaX-less conformation of the antenna and it is evident that this configuration is closer to the plant PSI inner antenna and thus can be considered the ancestral arrangement.
evidence: This is an inference about evolutionary relationships based on structural comparison.

claim: The conserved lipid binding by the PsaB loop close to PsaX is one of the most surprising findings.
source: One of the most surprising findings is the conserved lipid binding by the PsaB loop close to PsaX (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a structural finding from the crystal structure shown in Figure 6.

claim: The region of PSI near PsaX underwent the most drastic changes between Synechocystis and Thermosynechococcus.
source: This is the region of PSI that underwent the most drastic changes between Synechocystis and Thermosynechococcus, however the presence of the lipid is not affected by them.
evidence: This is a structural finding from the crystal structure.

claim: The presence of the lipid is not affected by the drastic changes in the region near PsaX.
source: This is the region of PSI that underwent the most drastic changes between Synechocystis and Thermosynechococcus, however the presence of the lipid is not affected by them.
evidence: This is a structural finding from the crystal structure.

claim: The function of the conserved lipid is related to assembly process of PSI, possibly to support reinsertion into the membrane after the synthesis of an extended stromal loop.
source: This suggests that the function of this lipid (and by inference the function of the other PSI lipids) is related to assembly process of PSI, possibly to support reinsertion into the membrane after the synthesis of an extended stromal loop.
evidence: This is a speculation about the function of the lipid based on its conservation.

claim: The absence of any sequence identifiable binding site for the lipid stems from the hydrophobic interactions made between its hydrocarbon tails and several chlorophyll molecules without involving any protein atoms.
source: The absence of any sequence identifiable binding site for this lipid stems from the hydrophobic interactions made between its hydrocarbon tails and several chlorophyll molecules without involving any protein atoms.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the crystal structure.

claim: Detailed structural information is significant in elucidating the biology of complex biological assemblies.
source: This highlights the significance of detailed structural information in elucidating the biology of complex biological assemblies.
evidence: This is a general statement about the importance of structural biology.

claim: A cluster of water molecules located between Fx and Q1B, conserved between Thermosynechococcus and Synechocystis was revealed.
source: A cluster of water molecules located between Fx and Q1B, conserved between Thermosynechococcus and Synechocystis was revealed.
evidence: This is a structural finding from the crystal structure.

claim: The two branches of the PSI ET chain are not equivalent, the PsaB located branch being faster.
source: The two branches of the PSI ET chain are not equivalent, the PsaB located branch being faster.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PSI electron transfer.

claim: The water cluster may modulate the contribution by Tryptophan PsaB 664 to the electron transfer between Q1B and Fx.
source: This water cluster may modulate the contribution by Tryptophan PsaB 664 to the electron transfer between Q1B and Fx.
evidence: This is a speculation about the functional role of the water cluster.

claim: The high structural conservation observed in the region around Fx implies that the final answers can only be reached using ever more detailed models and refined calculation methods which will include all participating atoms.
source: The high structural conservation observed in this region implies that the final answers can only be reached using ever more detailed models and refined calculation methods which will include all participating atoms.
evidence: This is a statement about the need for more detailed computational studies.
